article_5_text: processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject (‘lawfulness, fairness and transparency’);
recital_39_reference: Any processing of personal data should be lawful and fair. It should be transparent to natural persons that personal data concerning them are collected, used, consulted or otherwise processed and to what extent the personal data are or will be processed. The principle of transparency requires that any information and communication relating to the processing of those personal data be easily accessible and easy to understand, and that clear and plain language be used. That principle concerns, in particular, information to the data subjects on the identity of the controller and the purposes of the processing and further information to ensure fair and transparent processing in respect of the natural persons concerned and their right to obtain confirmation and communication of personal data concerning them which are being processed.

policy_clauses.quote: PLEASE READ THIS POLICY CAREFULLY BEFORE USING ADA HEALTH GMBH SERVICES.

This privacy policy (the “Privacy Policy”), together with our Terms & Conditions at ada.com/terms-and-conditions, our Cookie Policy at ada.com/cookie-policy and any other documents referred therein, sets out the basis on which any personal data we collect from you, or that you provide to us, will be processed.

Please read this Privacy Policy carefully to understand the types of data we collect from you, how we use it, the circumstances under which we will share it with third parties, and your rights in relation to your personal data.

This Privacy Policy applies to any personal data processed by Ada Health GmbH (HRB 189710), Neue Grünstraße 17, 10179 Berlin, Germany being the data controller (as defined under Article 4(7) GDPR) of all processing activities in connection with the Services.
Our data protection officer can be contacted at [dpo@ada.com](mailto:dpo@ada.com).
Before starting using our Services, you should read our Privacy Policy carefully.

In order to use our Symptom Assessment and other health related features, you have to consent to Ada analyzing the personal health data you voluntarily share in order to be provided with an assessment and health advice.

If you wish to read in detail all the data processing activities we undertake, we advise you to read the following section 3 relating to each specific data processing activity, and sections 4 to 9 that relate to: • our cookies & tracking policy (section 4), • where we store your personal data (section 5), • when we may disclose your personal data (section 6), • our retention policy (section 7), • your data subjects’ rights (section 8)...

When using Ada’s Services, you are not subject to a decision that is based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning you or similarly significantly affects you (automated decision-making, Art. 22 GDPR).
This Privacy Policy describes our data processing when using the App, Ada Assess, the Website or any service and/or product we may provide you (together with the “Services”).
3.1 When you access our Services • Use justification: Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f)GDPR).
3.2a When you register a user account or create a new profile • Use justification: Contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)GDPR / Consent (Article9(2)(a) GDPR) for the processing of your health data.
3.5 Symptom assessment and health related features • Use justification: Contract performance (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR / Consent (Article 9(2)(a)GDPR) for the processing of your health data.

4. Cookies and tracking on our Website ... This processing is carried out either on the legal basis of performance of the usage contract for our website for necessary cookies or your consent for voluntary analytics or marketing cookies.
5. Where do we store your personal data ... Your health data and other sensitive data will always stay in the EU.
6. Disclosure of your personal data ... Ada does not share your data for third-party commercial interests without your explicit consent.
8. Your data subject’s rights Under GDPR you have various rights in relation to your personal data (as listed below).
Any changes we make to our Privacy Policy in the future will be posted on this page, and where appropriate, notified to you by email, notifications via the App, or by any other available means.

justification: The policy provides extensive transparency elements highlighted in Recital 39 (identity of controller and DPO, detailed purposes, legal bases, retention, recipients, and data-subject rights), which supports compliance with Article 5(1)(a). However, several legal-basis presentations are potentially confusing (e.g., combining multiple bases within one activity and “you have to consent” framing), and some disclosures rely on layered external documents (Terms/Cookie Policy/linked lists), which can undermine the “easily accessible and easy to understand” requirement in Recital 39 for some users. ([gdpr-info.eu][1])

article_5_text: collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes; further processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes shall, in accordance with Article 89(1), not be considered to be incompatible with the initial purposes (‘purpose limitation’);
recital_39_reference: In particular, the specific purposes for which personal data are processed should be explicit and legitimate and determined at the time of the collection of the personal data.

justification: The policy states explicit, activity-specific “Purpose of processing” clauses across Section 3 (plus cookies, disclosures, and retention logic), aligning with Article 5(1)(b) and Recital 39’s requirement that purposes be “explicit and legitimate” and set at collection. It also describes limits on onward use (e.g., “we will stop using it for the purpose with the shorter period”) and treats statistical/public-health uses as pseudonymized/anonymized outputs, consistent with Article 5(1)(b)’s compatibility carve-out for statistical/scientific purposes when safeguards apply. ([gdpr-info.eu][1])

recital_39_reference: The personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed. Personal data should be processed only if the purpose of the processing could not reasonably be fulfilled by other means.

However, the policy also describes broad intake categories (including “phone number” and “further information required to verify your identity”) without consistently explaining necessity by purpose, and it sometimes relies on general assurances (“not intended to identify you”) rather than demonstrating that each data element is strictly necessary or could not “reasonably be fulfilled by other means.” ([gdpr-info.eu][1])

recital_39_reference: Every reasonable step should be taken to ensure that personal data which are inaccurate are rectified or deleted.

justification: The policy supports correction mechanisms by clearly describing rectification and restriction rights, which maps to Article 5(1)(d) and Recital 39’s instruction to rectify or delete inaccurate data. However, beyond user-driven updates and rights procedures, it does not describe concrete “every reasonable step” operational measures (e.g., periodic validation, prompts to update stale health profile elements, or accuracy governance for user-entered data), leaving the “kept up to date” expectation only partially evidenced. ([gdpr-info.eu][1])

article_5_text: kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed; personal data may be stored for longer periods insofar as the personal data will be processed solely for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89(1) subject to implementation of the appropriate technical and organisational measures required by this Regulation in order to safeguard the rights and freedoms of the data subject (‘storage limitation’);
recital_39_reference: This requires, in particular, ensuring that the period for which the personal data are stored is limited to a strict minimum. In order to ensure that the personal data are not kept longer than necessary, time limits should be established by the controller for erasure or for a periodic review.

justification: The policy sets multiple concrete time limits (e.g., 15/45/60 days, deletion/anonymisation within 1 month, and defined litigation retention), which supports Article 5(1)(e) and Recital 39’s expectation that controllers establish time limits for erasure/retention. However, several retention statements remain open-ended (“as long as necessary,” “corresponds with our obligation,” or “until it is no longer required”) without clear criteria or explicit periodic review procedures, which makes it harder to show that identification is kept to a “strict minimum” in all cases. justification: The policy describes multiple technical and organisational security measures (TLS in transit, EU hosting for sensitive data, ISO 27001-aligned controls, DPAs with processors, access restriction, and encryption/vaulting for retained litigation data), which directly supports Article 5(1)(f) and Recital 39’s emphasis on preventing unauthorised access and ensuring confidentiality. While it does not enumerate every control in detail, the stated measures and governance commitments are consistent with an “appropriate security” posture for health-data processing. ([gdpr-info.eu][1])

article_5_text: The controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, paragraph 1 (‘accountability’).
recital_39_reference: Recital 39 does not address Article 5(2) accountability; assessment is based on Article 5(2) alone.

justification: The policy shows several accountability signals (clear controller identification, DPO contact, processor DPAs, cross-border safeguards pathway, and references to structured security and regulated medical-device compliance), which supports “responsible for” compliance in Article 5(2). However, Article 5(2) also requires being able to “demonstrate” compliance, and the policy does not explicitly describe demonstrability mechanisms (e.g., records of processing, DPIAs for high-risk health processing, audit routines, or governance evidence), so accountability is only partially evidenced by the policy text alone. ([gdpr-info.eu][1])
